title_ar: حكم ما يسمى بــ " لحْجَابْ" واستعمال الجداول والأوفاق
title_en: The Ruling on What Is Called 'l-ḥjāb', and on the Use of the Grids and the Magic Squares
body_ar:
أطلب منكم توضيح الحكم الشرعي لما يسمى عندنا بــ "لحْجَابْ"، وهل يجوز استعمال الاوفاق أو ما يسمى بالجداول ؟؟.

الجواب أن لحجاب يطلق على بعض الرقى والتمائم ونحوها وهو اسم عام يشمل الصحيح والفاسد ففيه ما هو صحيح مثل الرقيا بالقرآن والحديث الصحيح، وفيه ما هو باطل مثل ما كان من السحر ومن علوم الشر علم الجدول فعلم الجداول والأوفاق كله من علوم الشر فلا يحل للمسلم الاشتغال به ولا تعليقه، واختلف أهل العلم فيما يحل السحر منه فقد ذهب بعضهم إلى جوازه لأنه نافع غير ضار ولأن الله تعالى يقول " فيتعلمون ما يضرهم ولا ينفعهم " فهذه خاصية السحر فهو يضر ولا ينفع، أما ما ينفع ولا يضر فهو ليس داخلا في تعريفه ولكن مذهب الجمهور أن ذلك لا يحل مطلقا وأن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أبطله بقوله: " من أحدث في أمرنا هذا ما ليس منه فهو رد"، وفي رواية لمسلم من عمل عملا ليس عليه أمرنا فهو رد".

فهذا ليس مما جاء به رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من عند لله فلذلك لا يشتغل به المسلم ولا يحل له الإقدام عليه.
body_en:
I ask you to clarify the ruling of the revealed law on what is called among us 'l-ḥjāb', and whether it is permissible to use the awfāq, or what are called the jadāwil??

The answer is that 'l-ḥjāb' is applied to certain incantations and amulets and the like. It is a general name covering both the sound and the defective. Some of it is sound, such as the lawful incantation (ruqyah) by the Qur'an and by sound hadith; and some of it is void, such as what belongs to sorcery, and — among the sciences of evil — the science of the grid. The science of the grids and of the magic squares (al-awfāq) is entirely among the sciences of evil, so it is not lawful for a Muslim to occupy himself with it, nor to hang it about himself.

The people of knowledge differed concerning that by which sorcery is undone. Some of them held it permissible, because it is beneficial and not harmful, and because God, exalted, says: 'and they learn what harms them and does not benefit them' — this being the distinguishing property of sorcery, that it harms and does not benefit, whereas what benefits and does not harm does not fall under its definition. But the position of the majority is that this is not lawful at all, and that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, invalidated it by his words: 'Whoever introduces into this affair of ours something that is not of it, it is rejected' — and in a transmission of Muslim's: 'Whoever performs an act that our affair is not in accordance with, it is rejected.'

So this is not among what the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, brought from God. Therefore the Muslim does not occupy himself with it, and it is not lawful for him to undertake it.

flags.context: أطلب منكم توضيح الحكم الشرعي لما يسمى عندنا بــ "لحْجَابْ"
options: keep the dialect form in transliteration as 'l-ḥjāb' and let the Sheikh's own definition carry it
flags.note: DIALECT TERM — NEEDS A FIXED RENDERING. l-ḥjāb is Hassaniya Arabic, the Mauritanian form of al-ḥijāb, and the questioner marks it as local ('what is called among us'), vocalises it, and puts it in quotation marks. It denotes the written amulet worn on the body. The one rendering that must be avoided is 'hijab' in its modern English sense of a woman's headscarf, which is a completely different thing and which an English reader will supply automatically. The Sheikh defines the word himself in his first sentence, so the transliteration is not left bare. Needs the Sheikh's office to fix a rendering for the whole corpus.

flags.context: the two practices the questioner asks about
flags.note: al-jadāwil is on the style guide's list of terms pending a fixed rendering (§13) and this record is its second occurrence in this slice — see also record 551, where the Sheikh treats jadwal and tarbīʿ as synonyms. al-awfāq is the standard term for the letter-and-number squares of the occult sciences and is not in the glossary at all. Both should be fixed centrally and the same renderings applied to 551 and 586 together.

flags.arabic: واختلف أهل العلم فيما يحل السحر منه
flags.context: the disagreement the Sheikh reports in the second paragraph
options: that by which sorcery is undone
the undoing of sorcery by sorcery (al-nushrah)
flags.note: IMPORTANT — RISK OF INVERSION, AND A PENDING GLOSSARY TERM. yaḥillu here is from ḥalla, 'to untie/undo', not from the ḥalāl root: the subject is undoing a spell, not making sorcery permissible. Option 3 is the reading an English translator is most likely to fall into and it inverts the passage completely. This is precisely the question the literature calls al-nushrah, which is on the style guide's pending list (§13). The Sheikh does not use the word nushrah here, so it has not been put into his mouth in the body; a reviewer should decide whether the site glosses it.

flags.arabic: فقد ذهب بعضهم إلى جوازه … ولكن مذهب الجمهور أن ذلك لا يحل مطلقا
flags.context: the two positions on undoing sorcery
options: keep both positions explicitly attributed, as reported positions
present the majority position as the Sheikh's ruling
present the minority position as still open
flags.note: The Sheikh reports both positions and their evidences without saying in so many words which he takes, though his closing paragraph ('this is not among what the Messenger brought … it is not lawful for him to undertake it') reads as an endorsement of the majority. Whether that closing sentence refers back to the undoing of sorcery or to the grids and squares of the first paragraph is genuinely ambiguous in the Arabic, because 'this' has two possible antecedents. The English preserves the ambiguity. A reviewer should resolve it, since it decides whether the Sheikh has ruled on al-nushrah at all.

Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.

The Qur'anic citation is given in the source between straight quotation marks and without a reference; the wording matches Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:102. The source's presentation has been kept rather than converting it to the curly braces of house style, since the source does not present it as a formal quotation.

The Sheikh attributes the second wording of the hadith of rejection to a transmission of Muslim's, and that attribution has been kept exactly as he gives it. He gives no attribution for the first wording.
The source spells الرقيا for الرقية and من عند لله for من عند الله; both preserved in body_ar.
'Sound' and 'void' render ṣaḥīḥ and bāṭil, used here of the classes of amulet, per the glossary.
